rules.classification: Spectroscopic classes and alert or messenger labels are different definitions and are not compared; two active classes differ when neither label refines the other (for example 'SN Ia' and 'SN Ia-91T' agree); an earlier value from the same provider is a revision.
rules.host: Two proposed hosts agree when their names match after case and spacing are ignored or one name is among the other's NED cross-identifications; otherwise they are an identity ambiguity. Association probabilities are not computed.
rules.photometry: Only exactly compatible photometry (same epoch, band, system, method, calibration and direct/difference state, two or more providers) is compared. The limiting magnitude or flux that a provider reports alongside a detection is that epoch's detection threshold, not a non-detection, and is not compared with the detection; a detection brighter than another provider's non-detection limit at the same epoch is a status conflict. A group is listed only when it is still inconsistent under these rules; at most 10 groups per event, most significant first.
rules.position: Two positions with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they are more than 2 arcsec apart; when one states an error radius, the separation is compared with 3 times that radius.
rules.redshift: Two redshifts with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 0.005 (about 1,500 km/s); transient and host redshifts are different definitions and are listed, not compared; host redshifts of differently named hosts are an identity ambiguity.
rules.revision: A retracted row, or a superseded row of the same provider whose value differs beyond the property's rule, is a revision or retraction; a revision within the rule is consistent; the earlier value stays visible.
rules.sigma: Two values that both state an uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 3 combined standard deviations (uncertainties added in quadrature; a stated position error radius is treated as one standard deviation).

rules.classification: Spectroscopic classes and alert or messenger labels are different definitions and are not compared; two active classes differ when neither label refines the other (for example 'SN Ia' and 'SN Ia-91T' agree); an earlier value from the same provider is a revision.
rules.host: Two proposed hosts agree when their names match after case and spacing are ignored or one name is among the other's NED cross-identifications; otherwise they are an identity ambiguity. Association probabilities are not computed.
rules.photometry: Only exactly compatible photometry (same epoch, band, system, method, calibration and direct/difference state, two or more providers) is compared. The limiting magnitude or flux that a provider reports alongside a detection is that epoch's detection threshold, not a non-detection, and is not compared with the detection; a detection brighter than another provider's non-detection limit at the same epoch is a status conflict. A group is listed only when it is still inconsistent under these rules; at most 10 groups per event, most significant first.
rules.position: Two positions with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they are more than 2 arcsec apart; when one states an error radius, the separation is compared with 3 times that radius.
rules.redshift: Two redshifts with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 0.005 (about 1,500 km/s); transient and host redshifts are different definitions and are listed, not compared; host redshifts of differently named hosts are an identity ambiguity.
rules.revision: A retracted row, or a superseded row of the same provider whose value differs beyond the property's rule, is a revision or retraction; a revision within the rule is consistent; the earlier value stays visible.
rules.sigma: Two values that both state an uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 3 combined standard deviations (uncertainties added in quadrature; a stated position error radius is treated as one standard deviation).

evidence_timeline.summary: In the past decade, time domain astronomy surveys across the multi-messenger spectrum have developed "alert streams" which circulate observational information in real-time to the wider astronomical community. Despite this being standard practice for optical, gamma-ray and gravitational wave time domain astronomy for several years now, this kind of infrastructure has not yet been deployed at-scale for radio telescopes. We are conducting a long-term monitoring program that targets the Rubin Deep Drilling Fields using the Australian SKA Pathfinder (ASKAP). The primary goal of this program is to provide serendipitous radio observations of all objects of interest in these fields, and circulate that information in as close to real-time as possible. In this manuscript we outline the survey plans and status, the infrastructure we have developed to disseminate this information and an initial data release comprising 5 months of ASKAP observations of each field (although only 3 months overlaps with Rubin) conducted on an approximately 10 day cadence with a noise level of $\sim 60\,μ$Jy. As part of this data release, we present updated high-cadence radio light curves to the tidal disruption event AT2018hyz and the supernova SN2024abfo along with the discovery of two new radio variables, a possible tidal disruption event ASKAP J095711.5+051205 and an in-progress extreme scattering event ASKAP J005026.4-422958. The scientific results from this program along with the infrastructure developed to acquire them will lay the foundation for the integration of future radio imaging surveys into the broader multi-messenger alert stream, leading the way for major facilities such as the Schmidt Observatory System and the SKA.
evidence_timeline.title: ASKAP Monitoring of the Rubin Deep Drilling Fields

evidence_timeline.summary: Binary physics is important as >60% massive stars form in some kind of interacting binary system. The identification of progenitor systems of stripped-envelope supernovae (SESNe) offers one means to directly constrain binary evolution pathways, with implications ranging from the evolution of massive stars to the integrated stellar light from distant galaxies. Although the method by which SESN progenitors lose their envelopes remains uncertain, growing evidence have been shifting the paradigm from single star models to binary models. In recent years, five direct detections of surviving companions to SESN have been detected. However, the sample size is still too small to be statistically meaningful. Since suitable candidates for this type of search are rare, each additional new data point carries significant statistical weight. Here, we propose deep WFC3/UVIS optical and UV imaging of the only suitable SESNe target for a deep companions search in Cycle 33: SN 2022jli, which already has strong evidence of having a surviving companion. As with other companion searches, we plan to detect or place meaningful limits on any surviving companion. We also propose one orbit each to obtain F555W astrometry on the recent SN2024abfo and SN2024iss for potential future follow-up companion searches. This study will utilize HST's unique UV capabilities and build a statistically significant sample that will advance our current understanding of binary evolution. Given the rarity of relevant events and the limited HST lifetime, acquiring these observations is critical.
evidence_timeline.title: Searching for the Survivor: Deep HST Imaging of the Explosion Site of SN2022jli

evidence_timeline.summary: We present photometric and spectroscopic data of the type IIb supernova (SN) 2024abfo in NGC 1493 (at 11 Mpc). The steroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert System (ATLAS) survey discovered the object just a few hours after the explosion and observed a fast rise on the first day. Signs of the sharp shock breakout peak and the subsequent cooling phase are observed in the ultraviolet and the bluest optical bands in the first couple of days, while no peak is visible in the reddest filters. Subsequently, in analogy with normal SNe IIb, the light curve of SN 2024abfo rises again in all bands to the broad peak, with the maximum light reached around 1 month after the explosion. Its absolute magnitude at peak is M<SUB>r</SUB> = −16.5 ± 0.1 mag, making it a faint SN IIb. The early spectra are dominated by Balmer lines with broad P Cygni profiles, indicating ejecta velocity of 22 500 km s<SUP>−1</SUP>. One month after the explosion, the spectra display a transition towards being He-dominated, though the H lines do not completely disappear, supporting the classification of SN 2024abfo as a relatively H-rich SN IIb. We identify the progenitor of SN 2024abfo in archival images of the Hubble Space Telescope, the Dark Energy Survey, and the XMM-Newton space telescope, in multiple optical filters. From its spectral energy distribution, the progenitor is consistent with being a yellow supergiant, having an initial mass of 15 M<SUB>⊙</SUB>. This detection supports an emerging trend of SN IIb progenitors being more luminous and hotter than SN II ones, and being primaries of massive binaries. evidence_timeline.summary: Here we report the ATLAS discovery of the transient ATLAS24qew (AT2024abfo) in galaxy NGC 1493 at magnitude m_o = 18.55 +/- 0.17. The last non-detection through forced photometry was on MJD = 60628.28. Forced photometry indicates that the transient is rising, and that we have a first 3 sigma detection on 60628.30. Spectroscopic classification is encouraged.

publication_revisions.abstract: In the past decade, time domain astronomy surveys across the multi-messenger spectrum have developed "alert streams" which circulate observational information in real-time to the wider astronomical community. Despite this being standard practice for optical, gamma-ray and gravitational wave time domain astronomy for several years now, this kind of infrastructure has not yet been deployed at-scale for radio telescopes. We are conducting a long-term monitoring program that targets the Rubin Deep Drilling Fields using the Australian SKA Pathfinder (ASKAP). The primary goal of this program is to provide serendipitous radio observations of all objects of interest in these fields, and circulate that information in as close to real-time as possible. In this manuscript we outline the survey plans and status, the infrastructure we have developed to disseminate this information and an initial data release comprising 5 months of ASKAP observations of each field (although only 3 months overlaps with Rubin) conducted on an approximately 10 day cadence with a noise level of $\sim 60\,μ$Jy. As part of this data release, we present updated high-cadence radio light curves to the tidal disruption event AT2018hyz and the supernova SN2024abfo along with the discovery of two new radio variables, a possible tidal disruption event ASKAP J095711.5+051205 and an in-progress extreme scattering event ASKAP J005026.4-422958. The scientific results from this program along with the infrastructure developed to acquire them will lay the foundation for the integration of future radio imaging surveys into the broader multi-messenger alert stream, leading the way for major facilities such as the Schmidt Observatory System and the SKA.

publication_revisions.abstract: Binary physics is important as >60% massive stars form in some kind of interacting binary system. The identification of progenitor systems of stripped-envelope supernovae (SESNe) offers one means to directly constrain binary evolution pathways, with implications ranging from the evolution of massive stars to the integrated stellar light from distant galaxies. Although the method by which SESN progenitors lose their envelopes remains uncertain, growing evidence have been shifting the paradigm from single star models to binary models. In recent years, five direct detections of surviving companions to SESN have been detected. However, the sample size is still too small to be statistically meaningful. Since suitable candidates for this type of search are rare, each additional new data point carries significant statistical weight. Here, we propose deep WFC3/UVIS optical and UV imaging of the only suitable SESNe target for a deep companions search in Cycle 33: SN 2022jli, which already has strong evidence of having a surviving companion. As with other companion searches, we plan to detect or place meaningful limits on any surviving companion. We also propose one orbit each to obtain F555W astrometry on the recent SN2024abfo and SN2024iss for potential future follow-up companion searches. This study will utilize HST's unique UV capabilities and build a statistically significant sample that will advance our current understanding of binary evolution. Given the rarity of relevant events and the limited HST lifetime, acquiring these observations is critical.

publication_revisions.abstract: We present photometric and spectroscopic data of the type IIb supernova (SN) 2024abfo in NGC 1493 (at 11 Mpc). The steroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert System (ATLAS) survey discovered the object just a few hours after the explosion and observed a fast rise on the first day. Signs of the sharp shock breakout peak and the subsequent cooling phase are observed in the ultraviolet and the bluest optical bands in the first couple of days, while no peak is visible in the reddest filters. Subsequently, in analogy with normal SNe IIb, the light curve of SN 2024abfo rises again in all bands to the broad peak, with the maximum light reached around 1 month after the explosion. Its absolute magnitude at peak is M<SUB>r</SUB> = −16.5 ± 0.1 mag, making it a faint SN IIb. The early spectra are dominated by Balmer lines with broad P Cygni profiles, indicating ejecta velocity of 22 500 km s<SUP>−1</SUP>. One month after the explosion, the spectra display a transition towards being He-dominated, though the H lines do not completely disappear, supporting the classification of SN 2024abfo as a relatively H-rich SN IIb. We identify the progenitor of SN 2024abfo in archival images of the Hubble Space Telescope, the Dark Energy Survey, and the XMM-Newton space telescope, in multiple optical filters. From its spectral energy distribution, the progenitor is consistent with being a yellow supergiant, having an initial mass of 15 M<SUB>⊙</SUB>. This detection supports an emerging trend of SN IIb progenitors being more luminous and hotter than SN II ones, and being primaries of massive binaries. Within the SN IIb class, fainter events such as SN 2024abfo tend to have cooler and more expanded progenitors than luminous SNe IIb.
